summary:
Lamentations is five poems over the destruction of Jerusalem, the city Babylon besieged, starved, and burned in 586 BC. Its Hebrew title is its first word, Ekah — "How": "How lonely lies the city, once so full of people!" (1:1). The poems describe the catastrophe from close up — gates deserted, priests groaning (1:4), famine in which the hands of "compassionate women have cooked their own children" (4:10). The book names no author; tradition ascribes it to Jeremiah, who lived through the siege, and the ancient Greek translation added an opening line saying so.

Chapters 1, 2, and 4 are acrostics — poems whose verses begin with the successive letters of the alphabet — with twenty-two verses each, one for each of the twenty-two Hebrew letters; the form is often read as grief given complete, A-to-Z expression. Chapter 3 triples the pattern to sixty-six verses, three per letter, and chapter 5 keeps the count of twenty-two but lets the alphabet go. In the central poem the book turns: "Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope: Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!" (3:21–23). The phrase "loving devotion" renders the Hebrew hesed, God's loyal, promise-keeping love; the hymn "Great Is Thy Faithfulness" takes its refrain from these verses.

The turn is not the ending. The final poem is a communal prayer — "Remember, O LORD, what has happened to us" (5:1) — and the book closes on a plea whose answer is left open: "Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return; renew our days as of old, unless You have utterly rejected us and remain angry with us beyond measure" (5:21–22). Jewish communities still read Lamentations aloud each year on Tisha B'Av, the fast marking the temple's destruction; by custom the next-to-last verse is repeated after the last, so the public reading does not end on rejection.
